Deciding what to delegate
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: To delegate means to hand a task to someone else.

Write the first **10 to 15 articles** yourself. This confirms that content marketing (publishing helpful articles that bring in buyers) works. Invest in a writing team only after the channel has shown results.
Extra writing is not needed at the start. **A few authoritative articles beat many generic ones.** Authoritative means trusted and expert. Do not outsource blog writing to Fiverr or iWriter.
(Fiverr and iWriter are freelance marketplaces, websites where you hire people for single jobs.)
**Write product descriptions and SEO content yourself**, or learn them from free training, before paying someone on Fiverr. SEO means making your pages easy for search engines like Google to find.
The training covers SEO in detail.

Grow the business beyond your own hands. Hire people to take over your daily tasks **one step at a time**. Start with writing, the easiest role to delegate. Then add email, design, editing and data entry.

**Outsource tasks you cannot do well yourself**, such as detailed mock-ups (rough sample designs) and graphics, once cash flow (money coming in and going out) allows. Start with rough mock-ups yourself.
Bring in specialists to reduce errors as the business grows.
Decide between doing an edit yourself and paying a freelancer. **Compare the hours** a first attempt takes with the freelance price. Learning a new editing app can take days.
So outsourcing simple tasks can cost less than the time they take you.

Outsourcing ad creative (the images and videos used in ads) to freelancers does not guarantee strong results. Learning video editing from scratch takes a long time. **Plan for both before relying on either.**

Dropshipping (selling products that a supplier ships straight to the buyer) needs fast content and product testing (checking whether a product sells). Do it yourself or with someone who can produce content quickly.
Deciding what to delegate (continued)
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: Or pay a freelancer to deliver **within 24 hours**.
**Keep the creative team separate from routine operations.** Copywriters (people who write sales text) need freedom to incubate (let ideas grow).
Their output drops when they are held to the same visible schedule as operational staff.
Creative and offer quality drive results more than campaign structure (how ads are set up). A winning creative makes the strategy matter much less.
**Test many creatives and offers continuously.** Creative testing is one of the largest parts of the job, whether done in-house or outsourced.
**Use VAs (virtual assistants, remote helpers) for repetitive tasks** such as social media, email, customer service and content curation (choosing and sharing content).
Hire them through platforms (online job sites) such as AppWork, or alternatives such as OnlineJobsPH. Focus your own time on strategy.
**Create a clear role split for every task.** The owner keeps strategy and final approval. The owner delegates the rest.
Vetting means checking people carefully before you hire them.
1. **Post a job** for a freelancer, such as a writer or video editor.

2. **Give the candidate a test piece of work.** A candidate is a person applying for the job.
3. **Hire the best candidate.**
4. **Start producing the first content piece** with them.
**Hire quickly and imperfectly** rather than after a long search. The first producer can be replaced later, once output (what gets made) starts.

Hiring a native English editor
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: **Hire a native English editor you respect** to review articles and emails written by non-native writers.
Judge the editor by reading their own writing for clarity, conciseness (using few words) and persuasion (ability to convince).
Savings only happen when the editor **works quickly**.
A native editor needs about **15 minutes** for a 500 to 600 word article. Then they do a second pass (a second review).
If an editor spends more than an hour on an article that short, something in the process is wrong.

p.t: **Do not spend time creating or editing images yourself.**

A freelance writer at about $30 per article was too expensive to fill 60 to 80 empty collection pages (pages that list a group of products). Hiring in-house or on a part-time contract was more practical for ongoing content.

Production roles and team structure: Roles when systemising content marketing (setting up repeatable steps)
**Writer: drafts articles from keywords.**
**Email copywriter: writes emails and is paid more than the article writer**, because the email list (the people who signed up for your emails) is the most valuable audience.

**Editor and project manager: reviews articles and emails**, and coordinates everyone. This can be a native US English speaker.
**Designer or illustrator: creates keyword images.**

**Data entry: uploads articles to the blog and enters emails into the email provider (the software that sends your emails). This is a lower-level role. It is estimated at three to four hours** of freelancer time.
**Quality assurance (checking that work is right): the owner's final review.**
A content team that produced about **7 articles per week** had 7 writers, 3 editors, 2 graphic designers and 1 data entry assistant.
The data entry assistant prepares search result research for writers.
Once consistent content has produced results for about **12 months**, you can grow in three ways. Publish more than 2 pieces per month.

Increase promotion of existing pieces. Or hire an additional person.
Output and promotion should keep rising. Do not hold them flat once results are visible.
Once consistent content has produced results for about 12 months, **raise output beyond 2 pieces per month**, or hire an additional person to keep growing.
Use a fixed two-month review to keep the content process running. Spend **at most about 30 minutes** per review adding research and ideas to the planner.
Spread one content writer across several stores (separate online shops). Work **one store at a time**, for about one to two months per store, until its collection pages are complete.
A backlog of 60 to 80 empty collection pages was expected to take about six to eight months at that pace. Estimate the backlog size before assigning the writer to a store.

Per-keyword article workflow
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t:
1. **Change to the next keyword** on the list.
2. **Writer drafts the article** and hands it to the editor.

3. **Editor edits the draft** and returns it to the writer.
4. **Writer rewrites the article** and hands it to the editor.
5. **Editor finalises the article** and hands it to the email writer.

6. **Designer delivers the initial sketch** of the keyword image.
7. **Owner gives feedback** on the sketch.
8. **Designer delivers the final coloured image.**

9. **Email writer adds the article link**, then writes the subject line and the email body.
10. **Data entry uploads the article** to the blog and loads the email into the email provider.
11. **Quality check:** confirm every step is complete, then send.
**Track every keyword** in a spreadsheet, with one row per keyword and one column per task. Put the team member's name in each column header.

Mark each completed handoff with an X.
Use the grid to find bottlenecks (places where work piles up). For example, **ten finished drafts** may be waiting for the editor.
Track each article in a shared spreadsheet, with one column per production step.
Add **a checkmark when each step is done.** This shows who is responsible for each step and where work is piling up, such as when an editor has a backlog.
**Outsourcing without a tracker hides where work is stuck.** For example, drafts may wait for editing, or articles may never get uploaded to the blog.
Without a per-keyword overview, you only notice the problem when the output is already missing.
Set up systems and **check results regularly**. Then revise processes (change the steps) when results fall short.
Process, people and product are the core elements of any business. Content is mostly a process and people challenge.
Video, creative and file management: Creative strategy stages
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: Creative strategy (the plan for ad visuals and messages) runs through **four stages**:
conception, planning, production and management. An ad has to pass through all four to be produced and tested properly.
**Conception: develop the ad concept through research** before anything is made. This is where the idea and style are chosen based on evidence.
**Planning: define how the ad will be put together** and which assets must be produced.
A plan is needed before any filming, creator briefing (instructions for the people making content) or design work starts.

**Production: the actual creation of content**, such as filming, getting material from creators or designing assets. A plan alone produces no ads.
**Management**, in order:

1. **Upload the ads** and confirm they are live.
2. **Check that the media buying is set up correctly.** Media buying means buying ad space and setting up paid ads.
3. **Assess the performance metrics** (the numbers that show how well each ad works) of each ad.
4. **Use the learnings** to feed back into the system. Learnings means what you learned from the results.
5. **Repeat the cycle**, improving the ads that worked and stopping the ones that did not.
Most brands do only conception and production. **Planning and management are ignored or done poorly.** Their ideas often appear at random times.
They are launched after scraping material together (gathering scraps in a rush). This makes it impossible to test the angles (the different ways of pitching) in an orderly way.
Closing the creative loop
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: **Measure what is launched** and how it performs. Use the analysis to suggest the next creatives.
Then brief them and contact influencers when needed. Each step should feed the next.
**Build new creatives by combining hooks (the first words or seconds that grab attention) and testimonials** (customer reviews shown in ads) from a large research list.
This lets you scale testing without filming each ad from scratch. Keep the research list growing so new combinations keep coming.
When one concept proves profitable, **make new scripts around it**, with small hook or detail changes. Keep investing in that concept.
Once a fresh creative set is tested weekly or bi-weekly (every two weeks), the winning concept becomes the one to push.
Creating resized static ad variants (still-image ads in different sizes) **can be delegated to a VA** once the process is documented. The resizing step is repetitive and does not need the owner.
**Brainstorm sessions should run weekly or biweekly** (every two weeks).
This lets creatives come up with ideas, test new ideas and identify emerging trends (new patterns just starting) to stay ahead of the curve.

Once one editorial page (an article-style sales page) converts (turns visitors into buyers), **reuse its structure for other products**. Change only the character, the problem, the expert and the product facts.
Keep the AIDA order (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action, the order of a sales message) and the 70/30 split fixed. Each new page then follows a tested pattern.
Once a sales letter or funnel (the path a buyer walks through) has proven a closing structure (the way it ends with a purchase), **reuse that structure for new offers.** Only the opening
and the body need fresh creative work.
**Use the awareness pyramid** (a model of how aware buyers are of the problem and your product) as a recurring check.
Use it across traffic-based work such as content marketing, pay-per-click advertising (paying for each click on an ad), retargeting (showing ads to people who visited before) and email marketing.
Do not use it only for conversion rate optimisation (improving the share of visitors who buy).

p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: Before building any new email sequence (a series of emails sent in order), retargeting campaign or content-based ad, **write the plan first**.
The plan covers what the message should say and when it should be sent. Repeat this step each time a new email idea, new product or new content piece is considered.
The plan makes the build faster and easier to hand to outsourced staff.
The target is to raise email volume to **two, three or four emails per week**. A founder cannot produce that volume by hand.
So modular building blocks (reusable parts you assemble) are needed to make it workable in daily operation.
Email marketing example: an email marketer was hired from onlinejobs.ph (a freelance job site). She was trained on your products and Klaviyo (an email software tool).
She then created campaigns she had never made before. She became an expert in your business through hands-on work.
**On-the-job training** is often more effective than hiring an "experienced" expert who will not adapt to your specific needs.
1. **Create one main project folder** with three subfolders: video, audio and assets.
2. **Store raw footage** (unedited video) and product footage in the video folder. Include stock footage (ready-made clips you buy or download).

3. **Store music** in the audio folder. Split it into sound effects and songs.
4. **Store graphics and photos** in the assets folder, in an imagery subfolder.

5. **Keep the final project files in a cloud folder** such as Google Drive (online storage). Keep a local synced copy (a copy on your computer that updates automatically). Do not keep them only in Downloads.
Moving or deleting source files after importing them (bringing them into the editing program) breaks the links in the project. Footage can then disappear when you reopen it.
**Store all media in a fixed location**, such as a cloud folder synced locally. Never rely on the Downloads folder.
**Keep raw editing project files backed up in the cloud**, so a project can be recovered if the local computer or drive fails. Store source assets in organised folders alongside the project file.
Link building delegation (continued)
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: Link building delegation
**Delegate** backlink building work, such as skyscraper outreach, to a VA (virtual assistant, a remote helper)
or a freelancer (a self-employed worker you hire for a job). A backlink is a link from another website to yours.
Skyscraper outreach means finding popular content, making a better version, and asking sites that link to the old version to link to yours.
**Written SOPs** (standard operating procedures, which are step-by-step written instructions) make it possible to keep building backlinks to the site on an ongoing basis.

Resource page link building (getting links from pages that list useful sites) and broken link building (replacing dead links on other sites with your page) can also be handed to a VA, assistant or freelancer.
These processes suit delegation **once the niche opportunities are identified**. A niche is a narrow topic or market.
Link building tasks such as spreadsheet work (data in rows and columns), email sending and follow-ups are simple.
They need no advanced English or specialist skills. **They can be outsourced at low cost**, unlike coding, development, content writing or creative work.

The outreach work (contacting other sites to ask for a link) is repetitive and manual.
It needs little specialist skill, so **a general VA** can usually perform it.
There is no need to pay a high-cost freelancer. The tasks can be added to an existing VA's workload.
Compared with classic one-by-one skyscraper link building, this system is **highly automated** and scalable (it can grow without needing much more work).

After setup, the ongoing time commitment stays small.
Most of the work can be outsourced.
Broken link checking can be outsourced to a VA at **about 5 USD per hour**.
The assistant runs the checker (a tool that finds dead links) on every content page (a page with written text) of a niche site.

Ownership and priority
p.s: Delegating content, creative and link building

p.t: If the owner keeps doing repetitive link building tasks personally, they drop down the priority list.

Tasks done by the owner are rarely completed.
**Consistent outsourcing** prevents this slide.
Outsource link building in this order:

1. **Perform** each link building task yourself a few times until you understand it.
2. **Once the work is affordable, write or record an SOP** for the task.

3. **Delegate** the task to a VA or freelancer using that SOP.
Existing VAs with spare capacity (unused working time) are a good first choice for link building tasks.

They can take on part of the work immediately.
This avoids hiring for a new role before the workload justifies it.
For a serious link building goal in a growing business, **hire a dedicated link building team member**, full time or at least part time.

Once content production runs steadily, more link opportunities appear.
A dedicated person speeds up progress.
Extensive outreach also builds industry relationships.

These relationships can lead to business partnerships, co-promotions (promoting each other's products), guest posting (writing articles for other sites), featured mentions and promotions to their audience.
In a long-term business, these relationships can **pay off well beyond the link itself**.

Organic social posting (unpaid posts) **shows that the brand is active and real** when customers search for it.
It is not a direct sales channel, so it does not bring many sales on its own.
Paid social (paid ads on social media) for high-ticket products (expensive items) often has minimal return on ad spend (money earned per dollar spent on ads).
Paid social also has a long payback (time needed to earn back the cost). **Outsourcing it is not recommended.**

Recurring weekly content formats posted on fixed weekdays build loyalty.
